item.title: Hirome Market: Kochi's Lively Food Hall — Guide
item.description: Hirome Market is the beating heart of Kochi’s food culture, a lively covered hall in the city centre packed with dozens of small stalls and communal tables where locals eat, drink and socialise from morning till late. The undisputed star is katsuo no tataki — bonito seared over a fierce straw fire until smoky outside and rare within, sliced thick and served with garlic, salt or citrus ponzu. Around it you’ll find sashimi, fried treats, dumplings, local sake and much more, bought from whichever stall tempts you and eaten together at shared tables in a warm, boisterous atmosphere.

item.title: Kochi Sunday Market (Nichiyo-ichi) — Guide
item.description: The Kochi Sunday Market, or Nichiyo-ichi, is one of Japan’s great street markets, a tradition over three hundred years old that fills a kilometre-long avenue leading to Kochi Castle every Sunday. Hundreds of stalls line both sides of the street, selling fresh local vegetables and fruit, pickles, plants and flowers, tools, antiques, street food and crafts — much of it brought in by farmers and makers from the surrounding countryside. Wandering its length is a wonderful window into everyday Kochi life, full of local colour, seasonal produce and friendly banter.

item.title: Tosa Whale Cuisine in Kochi — Guide
item.description: Kochi, facing the Pacific, has a centuries-old connection to whales and whaling, and whale meat has a place in traditional Tosa cuisine. Historic whaling towns dotted the coast, and dishes using whale — as sashimi, simmered, or in the local ‘harihari’ hotpot with greens — were once a familiar part of the regional diet. Today whale is a niche traditional food served at a small number of specialist restaurants, presented as part of Kochi’s culinary heritage.

item.title: Yosakoi Festival, Kochi: Japan's Great Dance Fest — Guide
item.description: Yosakoi is Kochi’s gift to Japan: a dynamic, modern dance festival born here in 1954 that has since spread across the whole country and beyond. Held every August, the Kochi Yosakoi Festival transforms the city into a stage as around two hundred teams — tens of thousands of dancers in dazzling matching costumes — parade and dance through the streets to pounding music that blends traditional and modern sounds. Each dancer wields naruko, small wooden clappers that click in rhythm, and every team choreographs its own energetic routine, competing for prizes across multiple venues.
